analysis.one_liner: Makes giant data centers pay the full cost of the grid upgrades built to serve them, with states losing federal highway money if they don't comply.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors on September 8, 2026, was referred to two House committees and has received no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require electric utilities to charge very large electricity customers — any facility or campus drawing 100 megawatts or more, typically data centers — the full, incremental cost of the generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades needed to serve them, even if the customer later cancels its contract. Before building such upgrades, utilities would have to make the large customer or its class pay the full cost. States that fail to adopt these standards would lose 100% of their federal highway funding. The goal is to prevent ordinary households and small businesses from subsidizing the massive power demands of data centers through their electric bills.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary electricity customers — households and small businesses — who today can be charged for part of the enormous grid upgrades built to serve data centers, and whose bills would no longer carry those costs. Utilities also gain a clearer legal basis to bill large customers for the dedicated infrastructure they require.

how_it_helps.text: It requires electric rates for large-load customers (100 megawatts or more at one site) to recover the full incremental cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrades needed to serve them, even if the customer later cancels its contract — so residents don't absorb those costs.

Before a utility builds an upgrade to serve large data center load, the utility must either require the data center to cover the full cost upfront through a contribution in aid of construction, or assign the full costs to the class of large-load customers.
States that fail to adopt the standard lose 100% of their federal highway funding, giving states a strong reason to act.

analysis.who_pays: Large-load customers — mainly data center and cloud computing companies — who would pay the full upfront cost of the grid upgrades built for them, and states that might lose highway funds if they refuse to implement the standard.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large data centers and cloud companies

drawbacks.text: The enforcement mechanism withholds 100% of a state's federal highway apportionment if the state does not implement the standard — an extremely heavy penalty that could cut off road and bridge funding for a state's drivers over a utility-ratemaking dispute.
Requiring large-load customers to prepay the full cost of grid upgrades could discourage some data center or manufacturing investment in a state, a cost supporters would have to acknowledge.
The bill preempts state utility regulators' traditional control over how rates are set, imposing a uniform federal formula on matters states have historically decided.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is well-targeted: making hyperscale facilities pay the incremental grid costs they cause protects other ratepayers and follows standard cost-causation principles. But the enforcement tool is badly mismatched — conditioning 100% of a state's federal highway money on its utilities adopting one federal ratemaking standard is an extreme lever that could defund road maintenance over a utility-billing rule, and in states that refuse, data centers might instead bear contract terms shaped under the threat of losing federal funds. The ratepayer-protection goal is sound; the mechanism is blunt and raises real costs of its own.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to two House committees, where it has sat with no cosponsors and no action taken.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 8, 2026, and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
No further action has been taken since the referrals; no hearings, markups, or floor votes are in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large data center operators are better off for now: no federal rule requires them to pay the full cost of the grid upgrades built for them, and state highway funding is untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data center operators avoiding new cost rules

for.name: Rep. Suhas Subramanyam
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 8, 2026, representing a Northern Virginia district dense with data centers.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no pattern of support or opposition has emerged yet.

industries.industry: Data centers and cloud/AI computing companies
industries.note: They would have to pay the full, incremental cost of the grid upgrades built to serve them — upfront or through their rate class — instead of those costs being spread across all electric customers. This directly raises their cost of siting large facilities.

Utilities gain a clear federal basis to charge large customers for dedicated upgrades (reducing their risk of stranded assets), but lose flexibility to structure deals that spread costs broadly. Ordinary ratepayers are the intended beneficiary.

industries.industry: State and local highway programs (in non-complying states)
industries.note: States that do not adopt the standard lose 100% of their federal highway apportionment, putting road and bridge funding at risk — a cost that would fall on drivers and construction contractors in those states.

analysis.trajectory: The bill was referred to two committees and has attracted no cosponsors, no hearings, and no committee action in the record. Bills introduced this late in a Congress with no bipartisan sponsorship very rarely reach the floor; the realistic path is that it dies when the Congress ends in January 2027 unless it gains cosponsors or a data-center cost controversy forces a hearing.
